answer_text:
Let

\[
M=\max_{x\in[0,1]}|f'(x)|.
\]

If \(M=0\), then \(f\) is constant and the endpoint conditions give \(f\equiv 0\), so the inequality is trivial. Assume \(M>0\).

For any \(x\in[0,1]\),

\[
|f(x)|=\left|\int_0^x f'(t)\,dt\right|\le Mx
\]

and similarly,

\[
|f(x)|=\left|\int_x^1 f'(t)\,dt\right|\le M(1-x).
\]

Hence

\[
|f(x)|\le M\min(x,1-x).
\]

Integrating over \([0,1]\),

\[
\int_0^1 |f(x)|\,dx
\le M\int_0^1 \min(x,1-x)\,dx.
\]

Now

\[
\int_0^1 \min(x,1-x)\,dx
=
\int_0^{1/2}x\,dx+\int_{1/2}^1(1-x)\,dx
=
\frac18+\frac18
=
\frac14.
\]

Therefore

\[
\max_{x\in[0,1]}|f'(x)|\ge 4\int_0^1 |f(x)|\,dx.
\]

So \(C=4\) works.

It remains to show that no larger constant can work. For \(0<\varepsilon<\frac12\), let

\[
a=\frac12-\frac{\varepsilon}{2}.
\]

Define

\[
f_\varepsilon(x)=
\begin{cases}
x, & 0\le x\le a,\\[4pt]
a+(x-a)-\dfrac{(x-a)^2}{\varepsilon}, & a\le x\le a+\varepsilon,\\[6pt]
1-x, & a+\varepsilon\le x\le 1.
\end{cases}
\]

This function is continuously differentiable, satisfies \(f_\varepsilon(0)=f_\varepsilon(1)=0\), and has derivative

\[
f_\varepsilon'(x)=
\begin{cases}
1, & 0\le x\le a,\\[4pt]
1-\dfrac{2(x-a)}{\varepsilon}, & a\le x\le a+\varepsilon,\\[6pt]
-1, & a+\varepsilon\le x\le 1.
\end{cases}
\]

Thus

\[
\max_{x\in[0,1]}|f_\varepsilon'(x)|=1.
\]

Its integral is

\[
\int_0^1 f_\varepsilon(x)\,dx
=
\int_0^a x\,dx
+
\int_0^\varepsilon \left(a+s-\frac{s^2}{\varepsilon}\right)\,ds
+
\int_{a+\varepsilon}^1 (1-x)\,dx.
\]

Using \(a=\frac12-\frac{\varepsilon}{2}\), this simplifies to

\[
\int_0^1 f_\varepsilon(x)\,dx
=
\frac14-\frac{\varepsilon^2}{12}.
\]

Hence

\[
\frac{\max |f_\varepsilon'|}{\int_0^1 |f_\varepsilon|\,dx}
=
\frac{1}{\frac14-\frac{\varepsilon^2}{12}}
\longrightarrow 4
\qquad\text{as }\varepsilon\to 0.
\]

Therefore, for any \(C>4\), choosing \(\varepsilon\) sufficiently small gives

\[
\max |f_\varepsilon'|<C\int_0^1 |f_\varepsilon|\,dx,
\]

so the inequality fails for that \(f_\varepsilon\).

Thus the largest possible constant is

\[
\boxed{4}.
\]
